# TCB Allowed List — Nanvix phys-mm

Any `external_body` outside this list must be removed.

## Allowed `external_body`

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/mod.rs::book_physical_memory_regions` — iterates a std
  `alloc::collections::LinkedList` via `for region in list.iter()`. The build
  toolchain's `vstd` (`/mnt/toolchain/verus/vstd`) ships ghost-iterator specs only
  for `slice`/`vec`/`VecDeque`/`BTree*`/`Hash*` iterators, **not** `LinkedList`, and
  the orphan rule forbids supplying `View`/`ForLoopGhostIterator` impls for the
  foreign `linked_list::Iter` from the `kernel` crate (E0117). Genuine Verus
  front-end limitation, not a proof gap or code bug — full analysis in
  `verus-unsupported.md`. The abstract booking effect is specified over
  `PhysMemView` and discharged (no `admit`) by
  `lemma_book_region_reserves_region_frames` in `mod.proof.rs`. `ensures` keeps the
  caller-relevant guarantee: allocator stays initialized and well-formed.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/mod.rs::book_mmio_regions` — same std-`LinkedList`
  iteration limitation as above. Abstract effect (skip-if-not-covered; book tracked
  frames) discharged by `lemma_book_mmio_skip_untracked` /
  `lemma_book_mmio_books_tracked`. `ensures` keeps allocator initialized and
  well-formed across booking.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref_mut`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::clear`- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc` — materializes a
  `&'static mut [u8; N]` from a backend-provided address (`usize as *mut`); raw-memory
  op Verus cannot verify without a `PointsTo` for the externally-owned `BssStorage`
  region. Mirrors `src/libs/raw-array`. `ensures` states alignment + in-bounds over
  the abstract `bump_view`.
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc_as` — delegates to
  `alloc` and re-materializes the slot as `&'static mut MaybeUninit<T>`; same rationale.
  `ensures` adds the `size_of::<T>()`/`align_of::<T>()` vs `(N, A)` guard arms.

## Skip / exclude from current proof target

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::get_mut`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::init`

## Allowed `external_body` — `frame::*` free-function shims (`frame.rs`)

The module-level `frame::*` free functions bridge the global allocator singleton
(`static mut INSTANCE`, reached via `instance()`) to the do-not-modify abstract
`phys_view()` / `FrameAllocView`. That bridge is a trust boundary identical in
character to the already-trusted `frame::book` / `frame::is_covered` /
`frame::alloc_range` shims: `phys_view()` is a zero-argument uninterpreted spec
function whose value cannot be tied to the `unsafe { INSTANCE.assume_init_mut() }`
static by any verifiable means. Each is `external_body` with a `#[verus_spec]`
contract stated over `phys_view()` and the returned frame values (monotone
post-state facts; there is no `old(phys_view())`). They were left unspecced when
`frame.rs` was the proof target because their sole consumer is `mm::phys::upool`;
they are specced here so `upool` can rely on them, and will be removed when the
frame singleton bridge is itself verified.

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::alloc` — draws a fresh frame from the global
  allocator. `ensures` (on success) page alignment, membership in
  `allocated_frames`, and refcount = 1.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::free` — releases one reference (last reference
  returns the frame to the free pool). Runs on `Drop`, so it has no precondition;
  `ensures` keeps the subsystem invariant on every path.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::share` — adds a reference to an allocated
  frame. `ensures` (on success) the frame stays allocated / refcounted.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::refcount` — pure query of an allocated frame's
  reference count. `ensures` (on success) the returned count equals the frame's
  refcount; (on failure) the frame is not allocated.

## Allowed `external_body` — `UserFrame::drop` (`upool.rs`)

`UserFrame::drop` releases the frame's reference by calling `frame::free` and, on
the error path, logs via the `error!` macro. The `error!`/`write!` expansion uses
`core::fmt` Debug formatting (`{:?}`), which Verus cannot translate to VIR
("Unsupported constant type"). The function is therefore `external_body`; its
`#[verus_spec]` contract is honored by trusting that body. The contract is not a
new guarantee — `ensures phys_view().inv()` is exactly the post-state already
established by the `external_body` `frame::free` shim it calls, and the logging
branch performs no state change. `opens_invariants none` / `no_unwind` record that
`drop` opens no invariant and cannot unwind (errors are logged, not propagated).

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/upool.rs::<UserFrame as Drop>::drop` — releases one
  reference on scope exit. `ensures phys_view().inv()` on every path.

## Allowed `external_body` — `PhysMemoryManager` (`manager.rs`)

`PhysMemoryManager` is a **stateless facade** over the global frame allocator
(`Upool` has no fields; kernel frames are drawn from the global `frame::*`
statics through `static mut PHYS_MEMORY_MANAGER`). Its target methods therefore
have no verifiable body: they mutate global `static mut` state, call un-specced
upstream allocator primitives, and use side-effecting combinators
(`inspect_err`/`and_then`/`ok_or_else`) and `error!`/`warn!` macros that are not
ghost-gated and have no `vstd` specs. They form a trust boundary identical in
character to the `frame.rs` shims: each is `external_body` with a `#[verus_spec]`
contract stated over the do-not-modify `phys_view()` / `FrameAllocView` and the
returned frame values (monotone post-state facts, as there is no
`old(phys_view())`). Abstract laws are carried by `manager.proof.rs` lemmas.

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::init` — writes the
  global `static mut PHYS_MEMORY_MANAGER` (`MaybeUninit::write`) and flips an
  `AtomicBool`. `ensures` keeps the allocator initialized and well-formed.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::alloc_user_frame` —
  draws a frame from the global allocator and wraps it as a `UserFrame`.
  `ensures` (on success) places the returned frame's address in
  `allocated_frames` and states page alignment.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::check_user_watermark` —
  reads the build-time `config::kernel::KERNEL_WATERMARK` and the global free
  count. `ensures` (on success) gives `spec_watermark_ok` and keeps
  `free_frames` finite.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::alloc_many_user_frames`
  — loop-allocates `count` user frames into a caller `&mut Vec`, with all-or-
  nothing cleanup. `ensures` gives `len == count` and each frame allocated on
  success, empty vector on error.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::alloc_kernel_frame` —
  like `alloc_user_frame` but yields a `KernelFrame`.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::alloc_many_kernel_frames`
  — like `alloc_many_user_frames` plus the contiguity guarantee
  (`kernel_frames_contiguous`) required for kernel stacks.

## Allowed `external_body` — not-yet-verified dependencies of `mm::phys::kframe`

`KernelFrame::new` is the first verified (`#[verus_spec]`) exec body in the proof
target that calls cross-module address-conversion / mapping helpers. Those helpers
live in `hal::mem` and `mm::virt`, which are **not yet verified**, so they are
declared outside any `verus!` macro and Verus would otherwise reject the call.
Each is given a temporary `external_body` `#[verus_spec]` contract so the verified
`new` body type-checks; the contracts are removed when their home modules are
verified. None weakens an existing guarantee — they only name facts `new` already
relies on (newtype address identity) or state nothing observable (the
identity-map side effect, which no `mm::phys` contract names).

- `src/kernel/src/hal/mem/types/address/frame.rs::FrameAddress::into_raw_value` —
  returns the frame's raw `usize` address; delegates through the `sys::mm::Address`
  trait. `ensures result as int == self@` (the newtype identity already assumed by
  `manager.rs`'s `kernel_frames_contiguous` reasoning). Removed when `hal::mem` is
  verified.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.rs::identity_map_page` — lazily installs a
  kernel identity-map PTE (page tables drawn from a BSS pool; no recursive frame
  allocation). The mapping side effect is not part of the physical-frame
  abstraction, so the contract states nothing abstract (`ensures true`). Removed
  when `mm::virt` is verified.

## Allowed `assume_specification` — `sys::mm::Address` trait method

`KernelFrame::new` also calls `<PageAligned<PhysicalAddress> as Address>::from_raw_value`,
a method of the external **`sys::mm::Address`** trait. A trait-impl method cannot be
given a standalone `external_body` contract without marking the whole trait `impl`
block verified (which would pull every sibling method into scope), so it is specced
with `assume_specification` in `kframe.spec.rs`. This mirrors the existing
`assume_specification` trust boundaries the codebase already draws at the
`sys`/`arch` library edge (`::arch::mem::PAGE_SIZE` in `frame.rs`, `Error::new` in
`libs/error`). The contract is trivial (the returned address value is not consumed
by any `mm::phys` fact); it is removed when `hal::mem` / the `Address` trait are
verified.

- `<crate::hal::mem::PageAligned<T> as crate::hal::mem::Address>::from_raw_value`
  (declared in `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.spec.rs`).

`phys_view()` / `FrameAllocView`. That bridge is a trust boundary identical in
character to the already-trusted `frame::book` / `frame::is_covered` /
`frame::alloc_range` shims: `phys_view()` is a zero-argument uninterpreted spec
function whose value cannot be tied to the `unsafe { INSTANCE.assume_init_mut() }`
static by any verifiable means. Each is `external_body` with a `#[verus_spec]`
contract stated over `phys_view()` and the returned frame values (monotone
post-state facts; there is no `old(phys_view())`). They were left unspecced when
`frame.rs` was the proof target because their sole consumer is `mm::phys::upool`;
they are specced here so `upool` can rely on them, and will be removed when the
frame singleton bridge is itself verified.

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::alloc` — draws a fresh frame from the global
  allocator. `ensures` (on success) page alignment, membership in
  `allocated_frames`, and refcount = 1.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::free` — releases one reference (last reference
  returns the frame to the free pool). Runs on `Drop`, so it has no precondition;
  `ensures` keeps the subsystem invariant on every path.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::share` — adds a reference to an allocated
  frame. `ensures` (on success) the frame stays allocated / refcounted.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::refcount` — pure query of an allocated frame's
  reference count. `ensures` (on success) the returned count equals the frame's
  refcount; (on failure) the frame is not allocated.

## Allowed `external_body` — `UserFrame::drop` (`upool.rs`)

`UserFrame::drop` releases the frame's reference by calling `frame::free` and, on
the error path, logs via the `error!` macro. The `error!`/`write!` expansion uses
`core::fmt` Debug formatting (`{:?}`), which Verus cannot translate to VIR
("Unsupported constant type"). The function is therefore `external_body`; its
`#[verus_spec]` contract is honored by trusting that body. The contract is not a
new guarantee — `ensures phys_view().inv()` is exactly the post-state already
established by the `external_body` `frame::free` shim it calls, and the logging
branch performs no state change. `opens_invariants none` / `no_unwind` record that
`drop` opens no invariant and cannot unwind (errors are logged, not propagated).

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/upool.rs::<UserFrame as Drop>::drop` — releases one
  reference on scope exit. `ensures phys_view().inv()` on every path.

## Allowed `external_body` — `PhysMemoryManager` (`manager.rs`)

`PhysMemoryManager` is a **stateless facade** over the global frame allocator
(`Upool` has no fields; kernel frames are drawn from the global `frame::*`
statics through `static mut PHYS_MEMORY_MANAGER`). Its target methods therefore
have no verifiable body: they mutate global `static mut` state, call un-specced
upstream allocator primitives, and use side-effecting combinators
(`inspect_err`/`and_then`/`ok_or_else`) and `error!`/`warn!` macros that are not
ghost-gated and have no `vstd` specs. They form a trust boundary identical in
character to the `frame.rs` shims: each is `external_body` with a `#[verus_spec]`
contract stated over the do-not-modify `phys_view()` / `FrameAllocView` and the
returned frame values (monotone post-state facts, as there is no
`old(phys_view())`). Abstract laws are carried by `manager.proof.rs` lemmas.

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::init` — writes the
  global `static mut PHYS_MEMORY_MANAGER` (`MaybeUninit::write`) and flips an
  `AtomicBool`. `ensures` keeps the allocator initialized and well-formed.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::alloc_user_frame` —
  draws a frame from the global allocator and wraps it as a `UserFrame`.
  `ensures` (on success) places the returned frame's address in
  `allocated_frames` and states page alignment.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::check_user_watermark` —
  reads the build-time `config::kernel::KERNEL_WATERMARK` and the global free
  count. `ensures` (on success) gives `spec_watermark_ok` and keeps
  `free_frames` finite.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::alloc_many_user_frames`
  — loop-allocates `count` user frames into a caller `&mut Vec`, with all-or-
  nothing cleanup. `ensures` gives `len == count` and each frame allocated on
  success, empty vector on error.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::alloc_kernel_frame` —
  like `alloc_user_frame` but yields a `KernelFrame`.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::alloc_many_kernel_frames`
  — like `alloc_many_user_frames` plus the contiguity guarantee
  (`kernel_frames_contiguous`) required for kernel stacks.

## Allowed `external_body` — not-yet-verified dependencies of `mm::phys::kframe`

`KernelFrame::new` is the first verified (`#[verus_spec]`) exec body in the proof
target that calls cross-module address-conversion / mapping helpers. Those helpers
live in `hal::mem` and `mm::virt`, which are **not yet verified**, so they are
declared outside any `verus!` macro and Verus would otherwise reject the call.
Each is given a temporary `external_body` `#[verus_spec]` contract so the verified
`new` body type-checks; the contracts are removed when their home modules are
verified. None weakens an existing guarantee — they only name facts `new` already
relies on (newtype address identity) or state nothing observable (the
identity-map side effect, which no `mm::phys` contract names).

- `src/kernel/src/hal/mem/types/address/frame.rs::FrameAddress::into_raw_value` —
  returns the frame's raw `usize` address; delegates through the `sys::mm::Address`
  trait. `ensures result as int == self@` (the newtype identity already assumed by
  `manager.rs`'s `kernel_frames_contiguous` reasoning). Removed when `hal::mem` is
  verified.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.rs::identity_map_page` — lazily installs a
  kernel identity-map PTE (page tables drawn from a BSS pool; no recursive frame
  allocation). The mapping side effect is not part of the physical-frame
  abstraction, so the contract states nothing abstract (`ensures true`). Removed
  when `mm::virt` is verified.

## Allowed `assume_specification` — `sys::mm::Address` trait method

`KernelFrame::new` also calls `<PageAligned<PhysicalAddress> as Address>::from_raw_value`,
a method of the external **`sys::mm::Address`** trait. A trait-impl method cannot be
given a standalone `external_body` contract without marking the whole trait `impl`
block verified (which would pull every sibling method into scope), so it is specced
with `assume_specification` in `kframe.spec.rs`. This mirrors the existing
`assume_specification` trust boundaries the codebase already draws at the
`sys`/`arch` library edge (`::arch::mem::PAGE_SIZE` in `frame.rs`, `Error::new` in
`libs/error`). The contract is trivial (the returned address value is not consumed
by any `mm::phys` fact); it is removed when `hal::mem` / the `Address` trait are
verified.

- `<crate::hal::mem::PageAligned<T> as crate::hal::mem::Address>::from_raw_value`
  (declared in `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.spec.rs`).

 `KernelFrame` is an **owned RAII handle to a single page-sized physical frame**
 allocated for kernel use and identity-mapped into the kernel address space. Its
 abstract value is exactly the frame's **base physical address** (`@ == base@`). The
 backing physical-frame pool is the `FrameAllocView` resource managed by the rest of
 `mm::phys`; a live `KernelFrame` corresponds to one address in that view's
 `allocated_frames`, and dropping it returns that address to `free_frames`.
 
 ## Key Invariants (caller perspective)
 - **Address identity:** `result@ == base@` after `new(base)`, and `base()@ == self@`
   always; the address is page-aligned and immutable for the handle's lifetime.
 - **Ownership transfer is all-or-nothing:** `new` takes ownership of `base` only on
   `Ok`; on `Err` the caller still owns/must-free `base`.
 - **RAII conservation:** every successfully constructed `KernelFrame` frees its frame
   exactly once on drop, preserving `phys_view().inv()`; drop never unwinds.
 - **Identity-mapped backing:** a live `KernelFrame` is safe to `clear`/deref within
   the kernel CR3 (established by `new`'s `identity_map_page`).

 - Source: none added by upstream callers. `kframe.spec.rs` and `kframe.proof.rs` are

   all unspecified).
 - View type: **exists** — `impl View for KernelFrame { type V = int; view = base@ }`
   is defined inline in `kframe.rs` (do not modify per task scope; it is not in the
   "do-not-modify" list but is already the right caller-abstract design).

 - Coverage: none yet — all three target functions need specs.
 - Strength: n/a (no ensures exist).
 - View design: **caller-abstract and adequate.** Downstream allocator contracts
   already consume `frame@` and `kernel_frames_contiguous(frames@, base)`, so an
   `int` base-address view is exactly what callers rely on; no field is biased toward
   a single caller. Recommended target specs: `new` ⇒ `result@ == base@` on `Ok` +
   no-consume on `Err`; `base` ⇒ `ret@ == self@`; `drop` ⇒ preserves `phys_view().inv()`,
   `no_unwind`, `opens_invariants none` (mirroring `frame::free`).

---
name: spec-design
description: "How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs."
---

# Spec Design Guide

## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles

### Qualities of a Good Spec

1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
   `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
   functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
   exec function (in-place). Never copy exec functions into a `verus!{}`
   block and spec the copy — that verifies the copy, not the real code.
3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
5. **Simpler than the code** — where the code has loops, the spec has `forall`;
   where the code has bit manipulation, the spec has `Set::contains`.
6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
   If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
   If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
   `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state.
8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
   writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
   directly into their proof. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely
   hides implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from
   inputs and return values through the module's public spec interface,
   `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.

### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria

If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
design model.

1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
   by the verification task (e.g., property analysis, human directive, or
   module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
   and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
   annotation beats no annotation.
2. **Write approved `assume_specification` first** — human-approved (`[x]`)
   items in the Needed Assumptions checklist are prerequisites. Write them
   before exec annotations so contracts can reference them.
3. **Cfg-gate sub-expressions, not whole functions** — one unsupported line
   does not excuse skipping the entire function's contracts.
4. **Reuse dependency specs** — check verified dependency spec files for
   existing `assume_specification` before claiming something is unsupported.
5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
   connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.

### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)

1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
   struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not add `ghost` or
   `tracked` fields to exec structs, change function signatures, or
   alter control flow. Specs must be purely additive.
2. **Verification Escape** — using `external_body`, `assume`, `admit`,
   or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
   spec or proof instead. `assume_specification` and `axiom` are trust
   boundaries — only permitted from the human-approved assumptions file
   (see Part 2: Spec Classification).
3. **Missing Loop Specs** — loops need `invariant` clauses that capture
   the loop's progress and preservation properties. A function with
   loops but no loop invariants has an incomplete spec.
4. **Code-as-Spec / Operational Spec** — restating implementation logic
   or describing computation step-by-step. Bad: recursive quicksort in
   spec. Good: `is_sorted(result@) && is_permutation_of(result@, input@)`.
5. **One-Sided Error Spec** — only specifies success, says nothing
   (or `true`) about failure. Error paths need equal rigor.
6. **Missing Frame Condition** — ensures says what changed but not what
   didn't. If a function modifies one field, the spec must state the
   others are preserved.
7. **Tautological Postconditions** — trivially true for any return value.
8. **Subsumed Properties** — logically implied by a stronger property
   already present (e.g., field-by-field ensures when a spec transition
   already covers them).
9. **Over-specification** — forcing a particular implementation strategy.
   Only add specificity when callers genuinely depend on it.

### Error Path Spec Principles

Every function that can fail should specify **what happens on failure**
with the same rigor as the success path.

1. **State Preservation** — on error, the state must not change.
2. **Bidirectional Failure Condition** — express error conditions as abstract
   predicates on the module's interface state, not as a list of individual
   code checks. Ask: what condition at the interface level makes success
   impossible?
3. **Liveness** — when preconditions guarantee success, state it
   explicitly only if it provides information beyond what the other
   ensures clauses already imply. Check whether the liveness clause
   is derivable (e.g., by contrapositive) from the error-path
   conditions — if so, it is redundant and should be omitted.

### Where NOT to Invest Spec Effort

**Completely skip** (no spec needed at all):
- **Type-system guarantees** — ownership, borrow rules, type matching
- **Display/formatting** — debug output, logging, string representation
- **Boilerplate trait impls** — derived traits, mechanical delegations

**Basic ensures only** (no additional spec design):
- **Trivial accessors** — field getters still need
  `ensures result == self@.field` for callers to reason about, but
  warrant no further properties.
- **Pure wrappers** — functions that directly delegate to a single
  verified function with no additional logic.

### Static vs Dynamic Condition Enforcement

**Key question**: Can this runtime check be statically eliminated through
verification?

**Yes → add `requires`**. The condition is provable from caller context
(e.g., index bounds derived from loop invariants, capacity checked before
insertion). The runtime check serves as a safeguard during development;
once all callers are verified, it becomes dead code and can be removed.

**No → keep runtime check + Err**. The condition depends on inherently
dynamic information (external input, hardware state, concurrent
operations) that no amount of static reasoning can discharge. A
`requires` clause here would be unsound or unusable.

**Guideline**: When both `requires` and a runtime check coexist, the
runtime check is a temporary safety net. Mark it as removable (e.g.,
`// TODO: remove once all callers are verified`) so that future
verification work knows to clean it up.

### Post-Generation Spec Refinement

After writing ensures clauses, review each one through the caller's eyes.
The guiding question: **could a caller who has never seen the implementation
find every ensures clause natural and directly useful?**

1. **Substitution test** — would this clause survive a reimplementation
   that preserves abstract behavior but changes internal strategy? If not,
   it encodes implementation detail and should be rewritten or removed.
2. **Minimality** — does this clause add information beyond what the other
   clauses already imply? Remove anything derivable from the rest.
3. **Direct usability** — can the caller use this clause as-is in their
   proof, or must they transform it first? If the latter, provide the
   form the caller actually needs.

---

## Part 2: Spec Classification

Specifications fall into three categories with different ownership:

### Internal

Specs that exist solely to help the verifier: helper lemmas, loop
invariants, intermediate assertions, proof-function pre/postconditions.
**The AI generates these freely during proving.** The test for
correctness is whether the code above can use them — the verifier
provides direct feedback.

### External-top (API contracts)

Public function `requires`/`ensures`, type invariants exposed to
callers, View types. These define **what the module promises**.
A human must review them for correctness and completeness.
Understandability is critical — a human auditor who cannot understand
the spec cannot approve it.

### External-bottom (trust assumptions)

`assume_specification` and `axiom` — assumptions about unverified layers
below (stdlib, hardware, FFI). **These are trust boundaries: if wrong,
everything above is unsound.** Only a human may approve these. The AI
must never write them on its own — if it discovers a need, it must
report it and wait for human approval.

### Rules

- Property analysis identifies external-top properties and reports
  needed external-bottom assumptions as a checklist (without writing code).
- A human reviews the checklist: approve items by checking them,
  reject by leaving unchecked, and optionally add notes or extra
  assumptions.
- Only approved assumptions may be turned into `assume_specification` /
  `axiom` code. Any unapproved use is treated as cheating.

---

## Part 3: View Abstraction Design

name: verus-constraints
description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers verus! block syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
---

# Verus Constraints

Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
constraints below.

## verus! { } Blocks Only

All spec and proof code **must** use native `verus! { }` block syntax.
Do **not** use attribute-based syntax (`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`).

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!

// ❌ WRONG — attribute style
#[verus_spec(ret => requires x < 100, ensures ret == x + 1)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 { x + 1 }
```

Even if existing code uses attribute style, write all new code in `verus! { }` style.
Attribute style is less mature; `verus! { }` can be auto-converted later.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Do not change
code logic; keep changes minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions, comments,
debug assertions, and all other existing code. If a construct is unsupported by
Verus (e.g. `debug_assert!`), cfg-gate it with `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]`
rather than deleting.

**Never cfg-gate away exec functions or impl blocks.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to an entire function/impl and providing a
verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the copy, not the real code,
and the two will silently diverge. Contracts must be added to the original
function in-place.

**Allowed additions:** `verus! { }` blocks (requires, ensures, invariants, decreases,
proof blocks, assert), vstd imports (cfg-gated), named returns `-> (ret: T)`,
ghost/tracked variables, `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**Never change:** semantic code logic or function/struct signatures. Exception:
only if Verus genuinely cannot express a construct — first search vstd for
alternatives, build a minimal reproducer proving unsupported, then make the
smallest change needed and document why.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must
confirm: (1) the code still builds with `cargo build`, (2) semantic code logic
is unchanged, (3) it is a genuine Verus limitation, and (4) it is documented.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Banned — only as placeholder in initial skeleton proofs |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | Banned — makes function an unverified black box. Verify the body directly or cfg-gate unsupported expressions. Exception: only if user prompt explicitly permits it |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — do not use to "fix" verification errors |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |

## assume_specification — Human-Approved Only

`assume_specification` and `axiom` are **external-bottom** trust
assumptions (see **spec-design** skill). They introduce
unverified axioms — if wrong, the entire verification is unsound.

**You must NOT write `assume_specification` or `axiom` yourself** unless
a human has explicitly approved them (e.g., via checked items in the
property analysis). If you discover a missing assumption, report it and try to specify it,
do not claim it as a required assumption or Verus's
limitation.

**Before reporting:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

## vstd & Common Misconceptions

Before writing custom specs, search vstd for existing ones (sequences, sets,
maps, arithmetic, pointers, atomics).

- **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
- **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
- **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.

## Claiming Verus Limitations

Before claiming any construct is unsupported, you **must**:

1. Search vstd (raw pointers, atomics, cells, locks, etc. are all covered)
2. Search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`
3. Cfg-gate the unsupported sub-expression — never skip an entire function
4. Build a minimal reproducer proving it cannot be expressed

Common false claims: raw pointers, `unsafe` functions, external types,
non-`verus!{}` constants, complex control flow — all handleable via the
steps above.

Partial contracts are always better than none. If 1 out of 5 clauses is
inexpressible, write the other 4.

---

# AST Consistency Check

Source exec code must not change during verification — see `verus-constraints`
for the full rules. This skill covers the **tooling** to enforce that guarantee.

## Tools

The checker uses tree-sitter to hash exec code after stripping all
ghost/proof/spec annotations. It detects changes invisible to textual diff.

`scripts/ast_consistency.py` provides four subcommands:
- `count` — quick pass/fail
- `summary` — per-element status table
- `diff --name "Fn::name"` — unified diff for one function/struct
- `report -o <dir>` — full report with all diffs

The `source` argument is optional. Use `--base-ref` to extract the original
from git, or omit both on `verus-ai/*` branches for auto-detection:

```bash
# Explicit original file:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py original.rs verified.rs count

# Via git ref:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py --base-ref main verified.rs count

# Auto-detect on verus-ai/* branches:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py verified.rs count
```

`diff` with `--full` shows specs; default is exec-only.

**MCP alternative**: If the `verus-ast` MCP server is registered, the same
functionality is available as tools (`ast_count`, `ast_summary`, `ast_diff`,
`ast_report`) with the same auto-detection.

## Pre-Approved Deviations

These minimal exec changes are known Verus limitations — no full deviation
process needed, but still document with a comment:

| Original | Verus Version | Reason |
|----------|--------------|--------|
| `self.x += 1` | `self.x = self.x + 1` | Compound assignment unsupported |
| `self.arr[i] \|= v` | `self.arr.set(i, self.arr[i] \| v)` | Mutable index unsupported |
| `-> T` | `-> (ret: T)` | Named returns for ensures |
| `#[derive(Clone, ...)]` | `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))] #[derive(...)]` | cfg-gating incompatible derives |
| `Ok(Self { .. })` | `let result = Self { .. }; Ok(result)` | Ensures needs to reference return value |
| `f(complex_expr)` | `let x = complex_expr; f(x)` | Intermediate value for assertions |
| `.ok_or_else(\|\| ...)` | `match ... { Some(v) => v, None => return Err(...) }` | Closures unsupported in some contexts |

## Handling MISMATCHes

When the checker reports a MISMATCH:

1. **Default: restore original code.** Exec changes are violations. Use
   `git show <base_ref>:path/to/file.rs` to view the original, then
   manually restore the changed exec code while keeping your annotations.
   Adapt the proof to the original code — not the other way around.
2. **Check pre-approved deviations.** If the change matches one above,
   keep it but add a comment documenting which deviation and why.
3. **Verify it's a real Verus limitation.** Before accepting any other
   change, confirm Verus genuinely cannot handle the original construct:
   - Search vstd for existing support (e.g. `checked_mul` has vstd specs)
   - Try alternative proof strategies that preserve the original code
   - Build a minimal reproducer proving the limitation
4. **If confirmed, document with full justification.** Add a `VERUS DEVIATION`
   comment explaining: what was changed, why the original doesn't work,
   what alternatives were tried, and why this is the smallest possible change.

name: bug-reporting
description: "Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug."
---

# Bug Reporting

Finding real code bugs is a high-value outcome of formal verification.
Not every verification failure is a bug — ensure you have genuinely attempted
to prove it first (see `proving-guide`) before classifying a failure as one.

## Classification

After genuinely exhausting proof attempts (see `proving-guide`), classify
every remaining verification failure into one of three categories:

**True Bug** — the code is wrong regardless of calling context. No reasonable
precondition could make it correct (e.g. arithmetic overflow on all inputs,
logic error that always produces wrong results).

**Context-Dependent** — the code looks incorrect in isolation but may be
correct given constraints enforced elsewhere (e.g. callers guarantee bounds,
a system invariant ensures uniqueness). Check callers, upstream module specs,
and system-wide invariants before concluding it's a bug.

**False Positive** — the code is correct but verification fails due to
spec errors (overly strong postcondition, wrong invariant) or solver
limitations (trigger issues, quantifier reasoning gaps).

## When to Report

- **True Bug**: report immediately. This is the highest-value finding.
- **Context-Dependent**: report with analysis of what constraints would be
  needed and where they might come from.
- **False Positive**: do not report — fix the proof approach instead.
  Never weaken existing specs (requires/ensures) to work around a verification
  failure; see `verus-constraints`.

## Report Format

Write findings to the bugs file (path provided in prompt context).
Reports will be read by human developers — use clear language, avoid jargon,
and make each report self-contained so readers need no additional context.

```markdown
## [True Bug | Context-Dependent] — function_name (file.rs:line)

**What**: one-line summary of the issue.
**Why**: root cause analysis — what the code does wrong and why.
**Verification Failure**: which clause failed (requires/ensures/invariant/assert),
verification command, and key error output.
**How Verus Helped**: how formal verification caught this bug (e.g. would it
be caught by testing? code review? why verification was uniquely effective).
**Severity**: safety-critical / correctness / cosmetic.
**Suggested Fix**: how the code should be changed.
```

If no bugs are found, write "None" to the bugs file.

name: verus-constraints

---

# Verus Constraints

Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
constraints below.

## verus! { } Blocks Only

All spec and proof code **must** use native `verus! { }` block syntax.
Do **not** use attribute-based syntax (`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`).

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!

// ❌ WRONG — attribute style
#[verus_spec(ret => requires x < 100, ensures ret == x + 1)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 { x + 1 }
```

Even if existing code uses attribute style, write all new code in `verus! { }` style.
Attribute style is less mature; `verus! { }` can be auto-converted later.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Do not change
code logic; keep changes minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions, comments,
debug assertions, and all other existing code. If a construct is unsupported by
Verus (e.g. `debug_assert!`), cfg-gate it with `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]`
rather than deleting.

**Never cfg-gate away exec functions or impl blocks.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to an entire function/impl and providing a
verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the copy, not the real code,
and the two will silently diverge. Contracts must be added to the original
function in-place.

**Allowed additions:** `verus! { }` blocks (requires, ensures, invariants, decreases,
proof blocks, assert), vstd imports (cfg-gated), named returns `-> (ret: T)`,
ghost/tracked variables, `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**Never change:** semantic code logic or function/struct signatures. Exception:
only if Verus genuinely cannot express a construct — first search vstd for
alternatives, build a minimal reproducer proving unsupported, then make the
smallest change needed and document why.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must
confirm: (1) the code still builds with `cargo build`, (2) semantic code logic
is unchanged, (3) it is a genuine Verus limitation, and (4) it is documented.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Banned — only as placeholder in initial skeleton proofs |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | Banned — makes function an unverified black box. Verify the body directly or cfg-gate unsupported expressions. Exception: only if user prompt explicitly permits it |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — do not use to "fix" verification errors |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |

## assume_specification — Human-Approved Only

`assume_specification` and `axiom` are **external-bottom** trust
assumptions (see **spec-design** skill). They introduce
unverified axioms — if wrong, the entire verification is unsound.

**You must NOT write `assume_specification` or `axiom` yourself** unless
a human has explicitly approved them (e.g., via checked items in the
property analysis). If you discover a missing assumption, report it and try to specify it,
do not claim it as a required assumption or Verus's
limitation.

**Before reporting:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

## vstd & Common Misconceptions

Before writing custom specs, search vstd for existing ones (sequences, sets,
maps, arithmetic, pointers, atomics).

- **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
- **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
- **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.

## Claiming Verus Limitations

Before claiming any construct is unsupported, you **must**:

1. Search vstd (raw pointers, atomics, cells, locks, etc. are all covered)
2. Search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`
3. Cfg-gate the unsupported sub-expression — never skip an entire function
4. Build a minimal reproducer proving it cannot be expressed

Common false claims: raw pointers, `unsafe` functions, external types,
non-`verus!{}` constants, complex control flow — all handleable via the
steps above.

Partial contracts are always better than none. If 1 out of 5 clauses is
inexpressible, write the other 4.

---
name: spec-design
description: "How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs."
---

# Spec Design Guide

## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles

### Qualities of a Good Spec

1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
   `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
   functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
   exec function (in-place). Never copy exec functions into a `verus!{}`
   block and spec the copy — that verifies the copy, not the real code.
3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
5. **Simpler than the code** — where the code has loops, the spec has `forall`;
   where the code has bit manipulation, the spec has `Set::contains`.
6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
   If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
   If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
   `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state.
8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
   writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
   directly into their proof. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely
   hides implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from
   inputs and return values through the module's public spec interface,
   `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.

### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria

If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
design model.

1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
   by the verification task (e.g., property analysis, human directive, or
   module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
   and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
   annotation beats no annotation.
2. **Write approved `assume_specification` first** — human-approved (`[x]`)
   items in the Needed Assumptions checklist are prerequisites. Write them
   before exec annotations so contracts can reference them.
3. **Cfg-gate sub-expressions, not whole functions** — one unsupported line
   does not excuse skipping the entire function's contracts.
4. **Reuse dependency specs** — check verified dependency spec files for
   existing `assume_specification` before claiming something is unsupported.
5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
   connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.

### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)

1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
   struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not add `ghost` or
   `tracked` fields to exec structs, change function signatures, or
   alter control flow. Specs must be purely additive.
2. **Verification Escape** — using `external_body`, `assume`, `admit`,
   or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
   spec or proof instead. `assume_specification` and `axiom` are trust
   boundaries — only permitted from the human-approved assumptions file
   (see Part 2: Spec Classification).
3. **Missing Loop Specs** — loops need `invariant` clauses that capture
   the loop's progress and preservation properties. A function with
   loops but no loop invariants has an incomplete spec.
4. **Code-as-Spec / Operational Spec** — restating implementation logic
   or describing computation step-by-step. Bad: recursive quicksort in
   spec. Good: `is_sorted(result@) && is_permutation_of(result@, input@)`.
5. **One-Sided Error Spec** — only specifies success, says nothing
   (or `true`) about failure. Error paths need equal rigor.
6. **Missing Frame Condition** — ensures says what changed but not what
   didn't. If a function modifies one field, the spec must state the
   others are preserved.
7. **Tautological Postconditions** — trivially true for any return value.
8. **Subsumed Properties** — logically implied by a stronger property
   already present (e.g., field-by-field ensures when a spec transition
   already covers them).
9. **Over-specification** — forcing a particular implementation strategy.
   Only add specificity when callers genuinely depend on it.

### Error Path Spec Principles

Every function that can fail should specify **what happens on failure**
with the same rigor as the success path.

1. **State Preservation** — on error, the state must not change.
2. **Bidirectional Failure Condition** — express error conditions as abstract
   predicates on the module's interface state, not as a list of individual
   code checks. Ask: what condition at the interface level makes success
   impossible?
3. **Liveness** — when preconditions guarantee success, state it
   explicitly only if it provides information beyond what the other
   ensures clauses already imply. Check whether the liveness clause
   is derivable (e.g., by contrapositive) from the error-path
   conditions — if so, it is redundant and should be omitted.

### Where NOT to Invest Spec Effort

name: bug-reporting
description: "Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug."
---

# Bug Reporting

Finding real code bugs is a high-value outcome of formal verification.
Not every verification failure is a bug — ensure you have genuinely attempted
to prove it first (see `proving-guide`) before classifying a failure as one.

## Classification

After genuinely exhausting proof attempts (see `proving-guide`), classify
every remaining verification failure into one of three categories:

**True Bug** — the code is wrong regardless of calling context. No reasonable
precondition could make it correct (e.g. arithmetic overflow on all inputs,
logic error that always produces wrong results).

**Context-Dependent** — the code looks incorrect in isolation but may be
correct given constraints enforced elsewhere (e.g. callers guarantee bounds,
a system invariant ensures uniqueness). Check callers, upstream module specs,
and system-wide invariants before concluding it's a bug.

**False Positive** — the code is correct but verification fails due to
spec errors (overly strong postcondition, wrong invariant) or solver
limitations (trigger issues, quantifier reasoning gaps).

## When to Report

- **True Bug**: report immediately. This is the highest-value finding.
- **Context-Dependent**: report with analysis of what constraints would be
  needed and where they might come from.
- **False Positive**: do not report — fix the proof approach instead.
  Never weaken existing specs (requires/ensures) to work around a verification
  failure; see `verus-constraints`.

## Report Format

Write findings to the bugs file (path provided in prompt context).
Reports will be read by human developers — use clear language, avoid jargon,
and make each report self-contained so readers need no additional context.

```markdown
## [True Bug | Context-Dependent] — function_name (file.rs:line)

**What**: one-line summary of the issue.
**Why**: root cause analysis — what the code does wrong and why.
**Verification Failure**: which clause failed (requires/ensures/invariant/assert),
verification command, and key error output.
**How Verus Helped**: how formal verification caught this bug (e.g. would it
be caught by testing? code review? why verification was uniquely effective).
**Severity**: safety-critical / correctness / cosmetic.
**Suggested Fix**: how the code should be changed.
```

If no bugs are found, write "None" to the bugs file.

name: bug-reporting
description: "Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug."
---

# Bug Reporting

Finding real code bugs is a high-value outcome of formal verification.
Not every verification failure is a bug — ensure you have genuinely attempted
to prove it first (see `proving-guide`) before classifying a failure as one.

## Classification

After genuinely exhausting proof attempts (see `proving-guide`), classify
every remaining verification failure into one of three categories:

**True Bug** — the code is wrong regardless of calling context. No reasonable
precondition could make it correct (e.g. arithmetic overflow on all inputs,
logic error that always produces wrong results).

**Context-Dependent** — the code looks incorrect in isolation but may be
correct given constraints enforced elsewhere (e.g. callers guarantee bounds,
a system invariant ensures uniqueness). Check callers, upstream module specs,
and system-wide invariants before concluding it's a bug.

**False Positive** — the code is correct but verification fails due to
spec errors (overly strong postcondition, wrong invariant) or solver
limitations (trigger issues, quantifier reasoning gaps).

## When to Report

- **True Bug**: report immediately. This is the highest-value finding.
- **Context-Dependent**: report with analysis of what constraints would be
  needed and where they might come from.
- **False Positive**: do not report — fix the proof approach instead.
  Never weaken existing specs (requires/ensures) to work around a verification
  failure; see `verus-constraints`.

## Report Format

Write findings to the bugs file (path provided in prompt context).
Reports will be read by human developers — use clear language, avoid jargon,
and make each report self-contained so readers need no additional context.

```markdown
## [True Bug | Context-Dependent] — function_name (file.rs:line)

**What**: one-line summary of the issue.
**Why**: root cause analysis — what the code does wrong and why.
**Verification Failure**: which clause failed (requires/ensures/invariant/assert),
verification command, and key error output.
**How Verus Helped**: how formal verification caught this bug (e.g. would it
be caught by testing? code review? why verification was uniquely effective).
**Severity**: safety-critical / correctness / cosmetic.
**Suggested Fix**: how the code should be changed.
```

If no bugs are found, write "None" to the bugs file.

106.    ensures clauses already imply. Check whether the liveness clause
107.    is derivable (e.g., by contrapositive) from the error-path

2. name: verus-constraints
3. description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers verus! block syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Verus Constraints
7. 
8. Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
9. constraints below.
10. 
11. ## verus! { } Blocks Only
12. 
13. All spec and proof code **must** use native `verus! { }` block syntax.
14. Do **not** use attribute-based syntax (`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`).
15. 
16. ```rust
17. // ✅ CORRECT
18. verus! {
19.     fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
20.         requires x < 100,
21.         ensures ret == x + 1,
22.     { x + 1 }
23. } // verus!
24. 
25. // ❌ WRONG — attribute style
26. #[verus_spec(ret => requires x < 100, ensures ret == x + 1)]
27. fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 { x + 1 }
28. ```
29. 
30. Even if existing code uses attribute style, write all new code in `verus! { }` style.
31. Attribute style is less mature; `verus! { }` can be auto-converted later.
32. 
33. ## Source Integrity (exec code)
34. 
35. The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
36. `*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.
37. 
38. Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
39. exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
40. constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Do not change
41. code logic; keep changes minimal so developers can review diffs easily.
42. 
43. **Preserve:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions, comments,
44. debug assertions, and all other existing code. If a construct is unsupported by
45. Verus (e.g. `debug_assert!`), cfg-gate it with `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]`

 # Verus Constraints
 
 Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
 constraints below.
 
 ## verus! { } Blocks Only
 
 All spec and proof code **must** use native `verus! { }` block syntax.
 Do **not** use attribute-based syntax (`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`).
 
 ```rust
 // ✅ CORRECT
 verus! {
     fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
         requires x < 100,
         ensures ret == x + 1,
     { x + 1 }
 } // verus!
 
 // ❌ WRONG — attribute style
 #[verus_spec(ret => requires x < 100, ensures ret == x + 1)]
 fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 { x + 1 }
 ```
 
 Even if existing code uses attribute style, write all new code in `verus! { }` style.
 Attribute style is less mature; `verus! { }` can be auto-converted later.
 
 ## Source Integrity (exec code)
 
 The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
 `*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.
 
 Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
 exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
 constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Do not change
 code logic; keep changes minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

 debug assertions, and all other existing code. If a construct is unsupported by
 Verus (e.g. `debug_assert!`), cfg-gate it with `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]`
 rather than deleting.

 `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to an entire function/impl and providing a
 verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the copy, not the real code,
 and the two will silently diverge. Contracts must be added to the original
 function in-place.

 proof blocks, assert), vstd imports (cfg-gated), named returns `-> (ret: T)`,
 ghost/tracked variables, `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

 only if Verus genuinely cannot express a construct — first search vstd for
 alternatives, build a minimal reproducer proving unsupported, then make the
 smallest change needed and document why.

 source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must
 confirm: (1) the code still builds with `cargo build`, (2) semantic code logic
 is unchanged, (3) it is a genuine Verus limitation, and (4) it is documented.

3. description: "Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Bug Reporting
7. 
8. Finding real code bugs is a high-value outcome of formal verification.
9. Not every verification failure is a bug — ensure you have genuinely attempted
10. to prove it first (see `proving-guide`) before classifying a failure as one.
11. 
12. ## Classification
13. 
14. After genuinely exhausting proof attempts (see `proving-guide`), classify
15. every remaining verification failure into one of three categories:
16. 
17. **True Bug** — the code is wrong regardless of calling context. No reasonable
18. precondition could make it correct (e.g. arithmetic overflow on all inputs,
19. logic error that always produces wrong results).
20. 
21. **Context-Dependent** — the code looks incorrect in isolation but may be
22. correct given constraints enforced elsewhere (e.g. callers guarantee bounds,
23. a system invariant ensures uniqueness). Check callers, upstream module specs,
24. and system-wide invariants before concluding it's a bug.
25. 
26. **False Positive** — the code is correct but verification fails due to
27. spec errors (overly strong postcondition, wrong invariant) or solver
28. limitations (trigger issues, quantifier reasoning gaps).
29. 
30. ## When to Report
31. 
32. - **True Bug**: report immediately. This is the highest-value finding.
33. - **Context-Dependent**: report with analysis of what constraints would be
34.   needed and where they might come from.
35. - **False Positive**: do not report — fix the proof approach instead.
36.   Never weaken existing specs (requires/ensures) to work around a verification
37.   failure; see `verus-constraints`.
38. 
39. ## Report Format
40. 
41. Write findings to the bugs file (path provided in prompt context).
42. Reports will be read by human developers — use clear language, avoid jargon,
43. and make each report self-contained so readers need no additional context.
44. 
45. ```markdown
46. ## [True Bug | Context-Dependent] — function_name (file.rs:line)
47. 
48. **What**: one-line summary of the issue.
49. **Why**: root cause analysis — what the code does wrong and why.
50. **Verification Failure**: which clause failed (requires/ensures/invariant/assert),
51. verification command, and key error output.
52. **How Verus Helped**: how formal verification caught this bug (e.g. would it
53. be caught by testing? code review? why verification was uniquely effective).
54. **Severity**: safety-critical / correctness / cosmetic.
55. **Suggested Fix**: how the code should be changed.
56. ```
57. 
58. If no bugs are found, write "None" to the bugs file.
59.

4. ---
5. 
6. # AST Consistency Check
7. 
8. Source exec code must not change during verification — see `verus-constraints`
9. for the full rules. This skill covers the **tooling** to enforce that guarantee.
10. 
11. ## Tools
12. 
13. The checker uses tree-sitter to hash exec code after stripping all
14. ghost/proof/spec annotations. It detects changes invisible to textual diff.
15. 
16. `scripts/ast_consistency.py` provides four subcommands:
17. - `count` — quick pass/fail
18. - `summary` — per-element status table
19. - `diff --name "Fn::name"` — unified diff for one function/struct
20. - `report -o <dir>` — full report with all diffs
21. 
22. The `source` argument is optional. Use `--base-ref` to extract the original
23. from git, or omit both on `verus-ai/*` branches for auto-detection:
24. 
25. ```bash
26. # Explicit original file:
27. python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py original.rs verified.rs count
28. 
29. # Via git ref:
30. python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py --base-ref main verified.rs count
31. 
32. # Auto-detect on verus-ai/* branches:
33. python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py verified.rs count
34. ```
35. 
36. `diff` with `--full` shows specs; default is exec-only.
37. 
38. **MCP alternative**: If the `verus-ast` MCP server is registered, the same
39. functionality is available as tools (`ast_count`, `ast_summary`, `ast_diff`,
40. `ast_report`) with the same auto-detection.
41. 
42. ## Pre-Approved Deviations
43. 
44. These minimal exec changes are known Verus limitations — no full deviation
45. process needed, but still document with a comment:
46. 
47. | Original | Verus Version | Reason |
48. |----------|--------------|--------|
49. | `self.x += 1` | `self.x = self.x + 1` | Compound assignment unsupported |
50. | `self.arr[i] \|= v` | `self.arr.set(i, self.arr[i] \| v)` | Mutable index unsupported |
51. | `-> T` | `-> (ret: T)` | Named returns for ensures |
52. | `#[derive(Clone, ...)]` | `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))] #[derive(...)]` | cfg-gating incompatible derives |
53. | `Ok(Self { .. })` | `let result = Self { .. }; Ok(result)` | Ensures needs to reference return value |
54. | `f(complex_expr)` | `let x = complex_expr; f(x)` | Intermediate value for assertions |
55. | `.ok_or_else(\|\| ...)` | `match ... { Some(v) => v, None => return Err(...) }` | Closures unsupported in some contexts |
56. 
57. ## Handling MISMATCHes
58. 
59. When the checker reports a MISMATCH:
60. 
61. 1. **Default: restore original code.** Exec changes are violations. Use
62.    `git show <base_ref>:path/to/file.rs` to view the original, then
63.    manually restore the changed exec code while keeping your annotations.
64.    Adapt the proof to the original code — not the other way around.
65. 2. **Check pre-approved deviations.** If the change matches one above,
66.    keep it but add a comment documenting which deviation and why.
67. 3. **Verify it's a real Verus limitation.** Before accepting any other
68.    change, confirm Verus genuinely cannot handle the original construct:
69.    - Search vstd for existing support (e.g. `checked_mul` has vstd specs)
70.    - Try alternative proof strategies that preserve the original code
71.    - Build a minimal reproducer proving the limitation
72. 4. **If confirmed, document with full justification.** Add a `VERUS DEVIATION`
73.    comment explaining: what was changed, why the original doesn't work,
74.    what alternatives were tried, and why this is the smallest possible change.
75.

17. 
18. ## Trait Obligations
19. - Trait: `View for KernelFrame` (defined inline in `kframe.rs`) — `type V = int`;
20.   `view(&self) == self.base@`. The abstract value of a kernel frame **is** the base
21.   physical address of the frame it owns. Allocator contracts in
22.   `phys/manager.rs` name returned frames purely through this `@` (e.g.
23.   `phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(frame@)`, the contiguity predicate
24.   `kernel_frames_contiguous(frames@, base)`). No caller inspects storage layout.
25. - Trait: `Drop for KernelFrame` — on scope exit the frame's base is returned to the
26.   global frame allocator via `super::frame::free(self.base)`. `Drop` must be
27.   `no_unwind` / `opens_invariants none` (errors are logged, never panic), matching
28.   the `free` shim contract in `frame.rs` (lines 762–779). Callers rely on this for
29.   RAII cleanup and rollback (see `alloc_many_kernel_frames`, `alloc_kpages`).
30. - Trait: `Deref` / `DerefMut for KernelFrame` — yield a `PAGE_SIZE` `[u8]` slice at
31.   the identity-mapped base. Out of scope (TCB), but callers like the kstack guard
32.   watermark code read/write through this slice; the CR3 safety invariant is the
33.   caller's obligation (documented in the impls' `# Safety`).
34. 
35. ## Caller Expectations
36. 
37. ### `KernelFrame::new(base: FrameAddress) -> Result<Self, Error>`  [`pub(super)`]
38. Call sites (real, exec-level):
39. - `phys/manager.rs:354` — `PhysMemoryManager::alloc_kernel_frame`: wraps a freshly
40.   `frame::alloc()`'d address; on `Err` it frees the raw frame (manual rollback,
41.   since no `KernelFrame` was constructed to drop).
42. - `phys/manager.rs:430` — `PhysMemoryManager::alloc_many_kernel_frames`: wraps each
43.   address of a contiguous run inside a loop, pushing successes into the caller's
44.   `Vec<KernelFrame>`; on failure it `frames.clear()` (dropping/freeing wrapped
45.   frames) and manually frees the un-wrapped remainder.
46. 
47. (The script's line numbers 253/302 for `new` point at `#[verus_spec]`
48. `requires`/`ensures` text on neighbouring trusted shims, not real call sites —
49. disregarded; the genuine constructors are 354 and 430.)

52.   - `frame@` equals the `base` that was passed in (the `@`/`base()` of the result is
53.     the input address) — needed so `manager` can assert
54.     `allocated_frames.contains(frame@)` and the ascending page-stride contiguity
55.     predicate over the returned run.
56.   - The frame is now identity-mapped in the kernel address space (so later
57.     `Deref`/`DerefMut`/`clear` are sound). This is `new`'s real side effect
58.     (`virt::identity_map_page`), but no caller depends on it abstractly — they only
59.     need the address-equality and the fact that the frame is now a valid owned
60.     resource that will free itself on drop.

63.     responsibility to free. Both call sites rely on this: they explicitly
64.     `frame::free` the raw address themselves on the error path. So `new` must NOT
65.     free `base` on failure (and indeed it does not — it returns before constructing
